units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content:
5.1. Failure to Maintain Proper Lookout.
5.1.1. International Regulations for Prevention of Collisions at Sea, 1972 (COLREGS) requires that “every vessel shall at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing as well as by all available means appropriate in the prevailing circumstances and conditions so as to make a full appraisal of the situation and of the risk of collision.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: 5.1.2. The mate of the PROWLER periodically left the wheelhouse to use the galley or restroom, leaving the vessel without a person in direct control and without a lookout. This was a routine practice aboard the vessel.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: 5.1.3. The PROWLER did not have a company or vessel policy that required a lookout to be posted in addition to the navigational watch officer, except in special circumstances. This left the navigational watch officer to also serve as the sole lookout.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: 5.1.4. At the time of collision, the mate of the PROWLER was the only person in the wheelhouse. Visibility was reported at approximately 6nm and their radar was functioning properly. Radar did not identify ATTESSA IV as a target, and the mate of PROWLER never visually observed the other vessel.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: 5.1.5. The ATTESSA IV was required by the Master's Standing Orders to have an assigned lookout on watch in addition to the navigational watch officer. The master directed the lookout to make a round of the vessel and secure the bosun's locker, removing the lookout from his station on the bridge.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: 5.1.6. The master of the ATTESSA IV did not observe the PROWLER visually or by radar until right before the collision occurred.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.sub_chunk: 5.2 Failure to Determine Risk of Collision
units.content:
5.2. Failure to Determine Risk of Collision.
5.2.1. Rule 7(b) COLREGS states, "Proper use shall be made of radar equipment if fitted and operational, including long range scanning to obtain early warning of risk of collision and radar plotting or equivalent systematic observation of detected objects.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.sub_chunk: 5.2 Failure to Determine Risk of Collision
units.content: 5.2.2. The PROWLER had a new radar installed approximately three weeks prior to the collision. The mate stated that the radar was operating properly and had displayed contacts earlier in the evening prior to the incident, however, the ATTESSA IV was never observed on radar.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.sub_chunk: 5.2 Failure to Determine Risk of Collision
units.content: 5.2.3. The ATTESSA IV was equipped with an X-band and S-band radar. Both radars had a collision warning alarm when a contact enters within the closest point of approach (CPA). The CPA had been set by the master to one mile. The master stated that the radars had been working properly when they departed San Diego, CA, but the master never observed the PROWLER by radar.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content:
5.3. Potential Radar Failure.
5.3.1. The operators onboard both vessels stated they were at their operating stations, alert, and maintaining a proper visual of navigation equipment and lookout. Both operators stated that their radar never displayed the other vessel in this incident. This would mean that in open water, during unrestricted visibility, at the exact same time, three different radars failed to detect the other vessel.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: 5.3.2. A post-casualty functionality test of the ATTESSA IV's radars was conducted by attending Coast Guard investigators. At this time, the radars identified close known targets as designed. Testing of the PROWLER's new radar was not completed due to extensive damage to the vessel and its equipment.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6.1. Determination of Cause. The initiating event for this casualty was the collision between the PROWLER and ATTESSA IV.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6.1.1. The operators of both vessels failed to use all available means aboard their vessels to identify if risk of collision existed, including visual and electronic means. The vessels both failed to have an additional lookout posted; the PROWLER did not require a designated lookout and although the ATTESSÀ IV did require a designated lookout, that individual was below decks doing other duties at the time of collision.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.sub_chunk: 6.2 The subsequent event for this casualty was the loss of propulsion aboard the PROWLER
units.content:
6.2. The subsequent event for this casualty was the loss of propulsion aboard the PROWLER.
6.2.1. After the PROWLER was struck by the ATTESSA IV, the PROWLER's engineering equipment sustained an unknown material failure that resulted in the loss of propulsion.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.sub_chunk: 6.3 The next subsequent event for this casualty was the flooding aboard the PROWLER
units.content:
6.3. The next subsequent event for this casualty was the flooding aboard the PROWLER.
6.3.1. The starboard hull of the PROWLER sustained a large hull penetration on the starboard side, resulting in the flooding of the engine and lazarette compartments. The vessel’s bilge and portable pumps were used to dewater the spaces and was able to keep up with the ingress of water.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6.4. The final subsequent event for this casualty was the personnel casualties aboard the PROWLER.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6.4.1. At the time of collision, a few passengers aboard the PROWLER were sitting in the galley. When the ATTESSA IV collided with the starboard side of the PROWLER, the galley cabin collapsed causing the death of one passenger and injury to others.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6.5. Evidence of Act(s) or Violation(s) of Law by Any Coast Guard Credentialed Mariner Subject to Action under 46 U.S.C. Chapter 77. The mate on the PROWLER allegedly violated law(s) or regulation(s) by violating the International Regulations for Preventing Collision at Sea, 1972 (COLREGS), specifically Rule 5 and Rule 7.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6.6. Evidence of Act(s) or Violation(s) of Law by U.S. Coast Guard Personnel, or any other person. No acts of misconduct, incompetence, negligence, unskillfulness, or willful violation of law committed by a person, including an officer, employee, or member of the U.S. Coast Guard contributed to the cause of the casualty, or to a death involved in this casualty.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6.7. Evidence of Act(s) Subject to Civil Penalty. There is no evidence that an act subjecting the offender to a civil penalty under the laws of the United States has been committed.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6.8. Evidence of Criminal Act(s). There is no evidence that a criminal act under the laws of the United States has been committed.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6.9. Need for New or Amended U.S. Law or Regulation. There is no need for new laws or regulations, or amendment or repeal of existing laws or regulations identified through this investigation, to prevent the reoccurrence of this casualty.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Actions Taken Since the Incident
units.content: 7.1. The ATTESSA IV changed the Master's Standing Orders to require the lookout maintain their position in the wheelhouse at all times.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 8.1. Safety Recommendations. None.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content:
8.2. Administrative Recommendations.
8.2.1. It is recommended that the findings in this report be forwarded to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, as the issuing authority for the master of the ATTESSA IV's merchant mariner credential and to the Cayman Islands as the Flag State of the ATTESSA IV.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 8.2.2. It is recommended that the Officer in Charge of Marine Inspections initiate Suspension and Revocation proceedings against the U.S. Coast Guard merchant mariner credentials issued to the mate of the PROWLER for allegedly violating laws or regulations in violation of the International Regulations for Preventing Collision at Sea, 1972 (COLREGS).

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 8.2.3. It is recommended that this investigation be closed.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant
units.content: The record and the incident investigation report completed for the subject including the findings of fact, analysis, and conclusions were reviewed and approved on October 20, 2022. The recommendations from the investigation are approved subject to the following comments.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 1: Recommend that the Commandant of the Coast Guard consider requiring life rings with lights on both sides of the main deck and searchlights in rescue boats as part of Title 46 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Subchapter K.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Action: I partially concur with the intent of this recommendation. The casualty on the vessel AMERICAN WEST (named QUEEN OF THE WEST at the time of the incident) does not indicate that additional lighted lifebuoys or requiring the carriage of a searchlight in the rescue boat would have likely resulted in a different outcome.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: The report of investigation (ROI) revealed that lack of crew training and accountability to company policies led to the crew member falling overboard from an area where multiple crewmembers were congregated, without handrails, where personal floatation devices were generally not required to be worn, and which was off-limits to crew at the time the man overboard casualty occurred. Further, the crew on deck displayed a lack of proficiency regarding how to respond to a man overboard scenario which would not be addressed by requiring the carriage of additional lighted lifebuoys, as highlighted by the crew neglecting to throw the vessel’s lighted lifebuoy or any flotation device into the water in the minutes after the crewmember fell overboard. The ROI indicated approximately 40% of the crew were not actively participating in man overboard drills nor receiving general training on the topic prior to the incident. Despite this, and although the rescue boat was not equipped with a search light, the crew was still able to launch the rescue boat within five minutes with two handheld flashlights.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Officers in Charge, Marine Inspection have authority under 46 CFR § 117.25(b) to require the carriage of additional lifesaving equipment (such as additional lifebuoys on a vessel with a relatively large amount of external passage areas for a vessel of its length, or additional loose equipment in the rescue boat) if they consider the regulations of Subchapter K to be inadequate for the conditions of the voyage. The Coast Guard recommends leveraging this authority in lieu of implementing changes to Subchapter K.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 2: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. test random crew members in Man Overboard drills annually. Coast Guard Marine Inspectors should plan to conduct a scheduled drill with the crew at the earliest convenience to the vessel after all temporary summer employees and deckhands have been hired and have had a chance to become familiar with the vessel.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 3: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. develop an inclusive safety policy with regard to all crew wearing life jackets while working in the vicinity of the stern. American Cruise Lines, Inc. should consider required personal protective equipment, safety practices, buddy systems, and/or tie-off system in developing their policy.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 4: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. assign all crew members a duty during a man overboard event and document these duties on the Station Bill.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 5: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. update the Station Bill to assign one crew member the responsibility of throwing the Man Overboard life buoy in event of a fall overboard. This person should have other duties on or near the bridge. All crew should be trained to throw anything buoyant immediately available to assist a person in the water.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 6: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. place a serviceable searchlight in the rescue boat.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 7: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. place a serviceable life ring in the port side main deck life ring bracket.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 8: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. provide floating lights for all main deck life rings.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 9: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. develop an inclusive safety policy with regard to authorized crew permitted to work on the stern in the vicinity of the paddlewheel. The policy should designate in writing the Authorized Persons permitted in the area. A physical list of authorized persons would deter others from accessing this dangerous area of the vessel and provide an effective tool to enforce the policy.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 10: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. provide physical barriers such as chains and warning signs on both sides of the vessel as visual deterrents to prevent unauthorized access to the stern.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 11: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc., in consultation with U.S. Coast Guard Marine Safety Unit (MSU) Portland Inspection Department, install effective deck lights (wired to the main deck lighting controls) on the stern portion of the vessel. In the meantime, it is recommended that P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST crew activate existing stern lights from sunset to sunrise every night.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 12: It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc., in consultation with U.S. Coast Guard Marine Safety Unit Portland Inspection Department, consider developing a locking mechanism to prevent the movement of the paddlewheel during swift current conditions. The mechanism should be developed only if the risk of damage to the paddlewheel support arms or associated vessel propulsion machinery is minimized.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 13: It is recommended that the Master of P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST provide survival training and Man Overboard training for all crew following a fall into the water.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 14: It is recommended that the Master of P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST ensure all crew actively participate in drills to ensure knowledge of man overboard recovery procedures.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 15: It is recommended that the Master of P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST actively enforce the Authorized Personnel Only policy to prevent others from accessing the stern of the vessel. Enforcement should include the use of effective and appropriate punishment and/or documentation of all personnel who violate the policy.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 16: It is recommended that the Master of P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST actively enforce all American Cruise Lines, Inc. Operations Manual policies onboard P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST, but most notably the following:

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: a. No drinking. Enforcement could include random alcohol tests when crew return from shore.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: b. Crew in quarters after midnight. Enforcement could include watchmen keeping track of who is not in quarters after midnight.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Recommendation 17: It is recommended that P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST's Engineer design (and put in place) a safety chain protecting authorized personnel on the paddlewheel support arms from falling from the stern in the area of the ten-foot railing gap.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant > Action on Recommendations
units.content: Action: I concur with the intent of Recommendations 2 – 17 which were issued to the AMERICAN WEST’s operating company and crewmembers. A copy of this investigation and its associated recommendations will be forwarded to MSU Portland and American Cruise Lines to locally resolve any issues of concern that remain unaddressed.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant
units.content: The record and the report of the investigation convened for the subject casualty have been reviewed. The record and the report, including the findings of fact, analysis, and conclusions are hereby closed.

units.parent_chunk: Action by the Commandant
units.content: The investigation's safety recommendations remain under review and consideration by the responsible Coast Guard program offices. The response to the recommendations and any resultant actions will be documented separately.

units.parent_chunk: Executive Summary
units.content: In accordance with reference (a) and (b) this Report of Investigation is prepared to document the circumstances leading to the loss of life following a man overboard from passenger vessel (P/V) QUEEN OF THE WEST, official number 1033572 on 07AUG2012.

units.parent_chunk: Executive Summary
units.content: On the morning of 07AUG2012 at 0111 hrs the Coast Guard received a distress call fróm P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST reporting that a member of the crew had fallen overboard. The vessel was moored at the marina in Rainier, OR in position 46-05.475N 122-56.886W. The crew of P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST immediately launched its rescue boat and called 9-1-1 to initiate a shore-side search. A Station Portland RBS and CGR 6035 helicopter were dispatched by Sector Columbia River to assist county sheriff's office vessels in the search. On-scene weather conditions were 62 degrees Fahrenheit, 8 nm visibility, 0 ft swells, 3-4 knot currents, and 7 knot winds at 300 degrees northwest.

units.parent_chunk: Executive Summary
units.content: P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST crew continued searching for an hour-and-a-half with the rescue boat and shore-side personnel with negative results. The rescue boat was recovered at 0235 hrs, half-an-hour after Coast Guard assets arrived on-scene.

units.parent_chunk: Executive Summary
units.content: At approximately 0400 hrs P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST departed from Rainier and continued her voyage to Stevenson, WA. Helicopter CG 6035 returned to base at 0435 hrs while the STA Portland RBS remained on-scene to conduct a first-light search. At 0835 hrs, the search was suspended and the RBS returned to base.

units.parent_chunk: Executive Summary
units.content: On 12AUG2012, two civilian boaters discovered the body of the crewman floating in the Columbia River channel in approximate position 46-11.35N 123-08.63W, 11 NM northwest of where the victim fell overboard. Cowlitz County Sheriff's Office deputies transferred the body to Cowlitz County Coroner's Office for cause of death determination.

units.parent_chunk: Executive Summary
units.content: On 09NOV2012, a Cowlitz County coroner indicated that the crewman died of asphyxia by drowning.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Deceased, Missing, and Injured Persons
units.content: Survivor Age Position Period of Employment

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 1. P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST (O.N. 1033572) is an inspected passenger vessel. The regulations that govern P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST are found in Title 46 Code of Federal Regulations, Subchapter K – Small Passenger Vessels Carrying More Than 150 Passengers Or With Overnight Accommodations For More Than 49 Passengers. P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST's last In-Service Inspection was conducted on 13APR12. Attending inspectors issued the vessel's Certificate of Inspection. The P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST was operated by American Cruise Lines, Inc. Captain was the master of the vessel at the time of the incident.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 2. At approximately 1200 hrs on 06AUG12 the vessel moored at the marina in Rainier, OR, for an overnight stay. The vessel's position was 46-05.475N 122-56.886W. Weather conditions were based on Captain| observations and historical information provided by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) website. On scene weather was clear with 8 nautical miles of visibility. The air temperature was approximately 62 degrees and the water temperature was approximately 69 degrees. Winds were 6 knots from WSW. The downstream currents were moving at approximately 4 knots. Tides were nearing the end of an ebb cycle and the tidal height was +2.00 feet above mean low low water (MLLW).

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 3. At 2140 hrs Mr. Staples signed off the vessel after working an entire shift and walked to El Tapatio Mexican Restaurant in Rainier, OR, where he purchased and drank two mixed drinks at the bar using cash. He took a photo of his drink and posted it to his Facebook page. When he consumed alcohol, Mr. Staples violated American Cruise Lines Operations Manual policy 3.3 (Alcohol Abuse / Alcoholic Beverages) which stated, "No member of the crew shall consume any alcoholic beverage while on board or ashore 12 hours before performing any duty, while they are in employ of American Cruise Lines and assigned to a vessel. Consuming any alcohol 12 hours before any duty is prohibited."

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 4. At 2201 hrs he arrived at Ol' Pastime Tavern in Rainier and consumed one bottle of beer that was purchased for him by another patron. He departed sometime around 2245 hrs.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 5. Mr. Staples signed back in to the vessel at 2246 hrs and joined other members of the crew in the dining room area to play video games until 0105 hrs. Some witnesses stated that he appeared intoxicated and slurred his speech. Mr. Staples and other members of the crew violated American Cruise Lines Operations Manual policy 3.6 (Crew Areas) which stated, "In no case will the crew be able to congregate in or use the dining room after 12 midnight."Additionally, Mr. Staples and other members of the crew violated American Cruise Lines Operations Manual policy 3.6 (Crew Areas) which stated, “All crew members, except those on duty, are to be in their quarters after 12 midnight."

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 6. At 0105 hrs on 07AUG12, Mr. Staples, two deckhands (Mr. and Mr. and the other galley steward (Mr. went out to the paddlewheel on the port side to smoke. By doing so, Mr. Staples and other members of the crew violated Captain standing order to not congregate on the stern of the vessel. However, there were no written policies onboard (or from the company) that prohibit such loitering on the stern. When questioned, witnesses were conflicted as to the policy: Some thought they could be on the stern to smoke, others knew it was against policy.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 7. At approximately 0105 hrs witnesses stated that Mr. Staples said that he was going "to take a piss" and approached the paddlewheel between the diagonal paddlewheel post and the ftermost bulkhead of the vessel. He was observed to stumble twice and attempt to grab the paddlewheel to steady himself.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 8. A red warning sign on the port side walkway approaching the stern stated, “Authorized personnel only beyond this point." The starboard side walkway approaching the stern had no such visual warning sign. Furthermore, there was no list of personnel authorized to access the stern on the vessel (or from the company).

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 9. Chains with red signs that said "Employees Only" protect passengers from approaching the stern on both sides of the main deck. On 07AUG12 and 09OCT12, visiting Coast Guard investigators found these protective chains hanging from the bulkhead of the vessel instead of in place across the walkways. Captain stated that policy required the chains to remain attached across the walkways, but that the crew often neglected to put them back in place when they went through. No written policy could be found to support Captain assertion.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 10. An area of 54 inches between the paddlewheel diagonal support posts and the aftermost bulkhead of the vessel was not protected by a railing or by a chain. This was the location where Mr. Staples fell in. An additional length of 10 feet on the port side stern was not protected by railings or other suitable guards to prevent someone from falling overboard. For additional detail, see Vessel Stern Schematic and Paddlewheel Support Arm Photo on pages 8 and 9, respectively.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 11. From December 2010 until May 2011, P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST underwent a complete propulsion system modification in which the entire stern was cut away and new bearing supports, deck plates, and a cosmetic paddle wheel were installed. MSU Portland Inspector was the lead Coast Guard inspector for the project. Mr. was the vessel's representative during the project.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 12. Plans were submitted by the Naval Architect Mr. of Chesapeake Shipbuilding and approved by Marine Safety Center. The plans did not indicate a railing arrangement, nor were there plans for a railing configuration onboard the vessel. The Marine Safety Center will review handrails only if the information is provided. According to lat MSC, "the designer provides [us] the overall construction of the vessel rather than details which are often left up to an outfitting decision: the owner may like the look of one handrail vs. another and that decision hasn't been made when construction begins."

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 13. On 04MAR11, MSU Inspector found the paddlewheel installed and indicated that all was satisfactory. During the project, Mr. and Mr. discussed the railing configuration and decided jointly that certain railings would not be included on the stern. As river debris frequently lodges in the paddlewheel planks, the risk of this debris getting caught in the associated railings outweighed the risk of someone falling overboard from the stern. The decision was made to make access to the stern authorized only to engineers working on the hydraulic machinery.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 14. There was an eye-hook on the aftermost railing stanchion. This stanchion was the last stanchion of existing railing before the 10 foot unprotected area on the port side stern began. According to Mr. the eye-hook was a connection point for a chain that was supposed to be designed to keep people away from the stern. The chain was not in place, nor had it ever been in place. Mr. assumed responsibility for not having the chain in place. Even if the chain had been in place on the night of the incident, it would not have prevented Mr. Staples from falling overboard, as he did not fall directly off the stern.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 15. An outdoor flood light was attached to the bulkhead above the machinery for the port engine on the paddlewheel support arm, but witnesses conflicted as to whether the light was on at the time of the incident. No other evidence exists to determine whether or not it was in operation. The light was wired on a separate switch from the rest of the deck lights so that it does not come into operation when the main deck lights are activated.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 16. The paddlewheel was "free-wheeling" and was turning slowly in the current in a counter-clockwise fashion when observed from the port side of the vessel. The paddlewheel has the ability to turn on its own when the vessel is moored in an area of strong current.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 17. Mr. Staples was unable to steady himself because the paddlewheel was "free-wheeling", and he fell into the water. He passed under or near the paddlewheel as the current carried him aft. He was wearing a tan jacket, white Adidas shoes, dark jeans, and a dark undershirt when he fell in. He was not wearing a lifejacket.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 18. Witnesses stated that Mr. Staples was conscious when he emerged on the surface of the water around ten seconds later. He was moving his arms slowly in the water back and forth. His eyes were open and he had a surprised expression. He was facing the vessel and did not shout for help.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 19. Mr. ran to get a life jacket from the storage box near the stern. He returned to find that Mr. Staples was too far away to throw it to him. He gave it to Mr. and ran to the dining room to alert the crew there. He then proceeded up the interior stairwell to the 4th Deck to alert the Captain and the Mate.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 20. Mr. ran forward along the port side walkway to the forward stairwell. He went up the stairwell to the 4th Deck and alerted the Captain. He then grabbed a lighted life ring and took it to the rescue boat to begin his man overboard duties of readying the rescue boat for deployment.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 21. There was an empty life ring bracket on the port side main deck walkway that Mr. ran past. This life ring bracket was approximately 40 feet from where Mr. Staples fell overboard. A life ring formally occupied the empty bracket, but according to Captain the company removed the life ring prior to the incident when it began to deteriorate.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 22. On 27APR2011 MSU Portland Inspector examined all the life rings onboard the vessel during the propulsion modification project. He noted that, "Only a few were acceptable. Most need retro reflective tape. Several had deteriorating grab lines (UV damage), and one was split open. [Mr.] directed the port engineer to have crew staff have the 5 required ring buoys prepared for inspection." Inspectors did not issue a CG-835 deficiency for the life rings. And there is no indication in the inspection report that the life rings were checked after being serviced.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 23. Mr. the vessel's engineer overseeing the project, removed the life ring that was split open (port side main deck) from service. He did not replace the life ring with a new one. The vessel's Certificate of Inspection (COI) required three life rings. The vessel had four life rings onboard at the time of the fall overboard. The vessel was abiding by the conditions of its COI.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 24. The vessel's Station Bill did not indicate that a life ring with a light should be thrown in the water to mark the position of the man overboard and/or provide the victim with a flotation device.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 25. Man Overboard (MOB) training was last conducted on 19JUL12 and the last drill was on 09JUL12. Only Mr. Mr. and the other deckhands participated in MOB training and drills. Mr. a galley steward) stated that he did not know how to respond when Mr. Staples fell overboard.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 26. On 07AUG12, Captain was awakened at 0108 hrs and immediately gave the order to launch the rescue boat. The mate (Mr. and the engineer (Mr. were assigned as crew for the rescue boat.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 27. The rescue boat had a compartment labeled "Searchlight" but did not have a searchlight onboard. Mr. ran from the Main Deck to the 4th Deck Bridge to obtain flashlights for the rescue boat crew to use while searching.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 28. At about 0110 hrs, the rescue boat was launched.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 29. At 0111 hrs Captain contacted the Coast Guard via VHF Ch. 16 and then called 911 by cell phone.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 30. At 0116 hrs a Fire and Rescue Truck arrived and began searching the shore line.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 31. At 0204 hrs, the Coast Guard helicopter CG 6035 arrived on-scene and began its search. The Coast Guard helicopter requested the crew throw a lighted life ring in the water for datum collection purposes. Captain threw a lighted life ring in the water. This was the first buoyant object to enter the water since Mr. Staples fell overboard.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 32. At 0235 hrs, the vessel's crew recovered the rescue boat. The rescue boat crew found Mr. Staples'tan jacket floating in the water.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 33. At 0400 hrs, Captain conducted alcohol breathalyzer testing for the six crew members directly involved. All results were negative for alcohol.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 34. P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST departed from Rainier, OR at 0454 hrs to continue its voyage.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 35. On 08AUG12 at 1130 hrs, the three witnesses present when Mr. Staples fell overboard were drug tested at Hood River, OR. All drug tests were later confirmed "negative" by a Medical Review Officer.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 36. On 12AUG12 at 0624 hrs, two civilian boaters found Mr. Staples' body in the Columbia River channel in approximate position 46-11.3N 123-08.63W, 11 NM northwest of where he entered the water.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Findings of Fact
units.content: 37. On 09NOV12, Cowlitz County Coroner indicated that Mr. Staples died of asphyxia by drowning. His death was ruled as an accident. Toxicology specimens were unattainable due to the advanced state of decomposition that Andres Staples presented.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: 1. Policies: American Cruise Lines, Inc. implemented a number of policies designed to protect crewmembers from harm onboard their vessels; namely, the "Crew in Quarters After Midnight, No Smoking Onboard the Vessel, and No Alcohol Policies". Mr. Staples violated each of these policies on the night of 06 August 2012 and early morning of 07 August 2012. Had Mr. Staples been in his quarters by midnight, he would have not been in a position to fall overboard. Likewise, if he had abided by company policy and gone to shore to smoke, instead of the stern, he probably would not have fallen overboard. Had he refrained from drinking that night, he may have acted with better judgment than to approach a dangerous area of the vessel.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Even though American Cruise Lines, Inc. made an effort to require crew to take certain safety precautions, the implementation of a number of additional policies will help prevent this kind of accident in the future. Namely, American Cruise Lines, Inc. has no formal, written lifejacket policy for their crews to follow. Captain stated that crewmembers were only told to wear lifejackets while working lines for mooring and unmooring. Had a stronger safety culture with respect to lifejackets been in place and enforced, Mr. Staples and his fellow crewmembers may have worn lifejackets out on deck in the early morning of 07 August 2012. Additionally, a written policy detailing which crewmembers were specifically granted access to the stern paddlewheel support arms (and for what reasons) will assist the Captain in enforcing the lax “Authorized Personnel Only" policy. Inadequate enforcement of this particular rule on the part of vessel management contributed to Mr. Staples (and other crewmembers) believing that access to this particularly dangerous area of the vessel was permitted despite the posted signage.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Safety policies are effected in order to thwart a passenger's or a crewmember's lapse of judgment. Investigators visiting P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST saw definite areas where the implementation of additional policies could save lives. But vessel managers must be willing and able to enforce policies effectively. Reprimands and documentation of transgressors coupled with strong leadership and continuous safety training will help vessel management ensure crew follow all company policies and will ultimately lead to heightened safety.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: 2. Barricades and railings: Investígators also noted an insufficiency of physical barricades to prevent crew and passengers alike from accessing the stern. "Employees Only" signs on main deck chains were provided to restrict passenger access to the forward main deck areas only. But on two separate visits to the vessel by investigators, they were not being used to deter passenger access. Most notably, there was a complete absence of physical barriers to prevent the crew from approaching the stern, though ample opportunity existed to put an effective barricade system in place. A simple chain (with a similar warning sign as that used for passengers) attached to the bulkhead and stretched across the walkway in the bottleneck area of the main deck immediately forward of the paddlewheel support arms would suffice as a clear reminder to crew that the paddlewheel support arms are off-limits. Finally, investigators discovered an eye-ring connection on the aftermost railing designe to provide a point of attachment for a grab line or chain to protect personnel working on the paddlewheel support arms from accidentally falling directly off the stern. The grab line or chain had never been placed into service, but vessel personnel stated they could manufacture one very easily.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Historical records and photographs of the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST show railings extending all the way to the afterimost portion of the vessel. When investigators arrived onboard, they noted that there were two segments on the port side paddlewheel support arm unprotected without railings: a 54-inch section (where Mr. Staples fell) between the wheel and the aftermost bulkhead of the accommodation bulkhead, and a 10-foot section along the aftermost stretch of the arm (see diagram below for details on unprotected railing areas). The hydraulic turning gear for the original, functional paddlewheel was arranged to prevent someone from easily accessing the extreme end of the vessel, even though historical photographs show that railing existed beyond the turning gear. Historical photographs also show that the 54-inch area where the paddlewheel diagonal supports attach to the aftermost exterior bulkhead was unprotected. Complicating this investigation was the fact that an official railing diagram or schematic was not created during the cosmetic paddlewheel installation project: Investigators had to rely on photographs of the vessel before the re-fit project and statements from involved parties.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Red dotted lines indicate proposed Mr. Staples fell overboard from this position barrier positions for restricting access between the bulkead and the paddlewheel. to the stern.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: According to the attending Coast Guard inspector, it was determined during the cosmetic paddlewheel installation project that railings in this area of the vessel would only become a larger safety concern due to the possibility of river debris being carried up with the paddlewheel boards and becoming lodged between the paddlewheel and the railings, causing potential damage to the wheel or the propulsion gear located in the vicinity of the stern. The threat of damage to the propulsion system outweighed the threat of personnel falling overboard. As a precaution, Coast Guard inspectors and vessel representatives decided to make the paddlewheel support arms an “Authorized Personnel Only" area. Since the stern was to be accessible by authorized personnel only, the requirement for railings was waived as neither passengers nor unauthorized crew were permitted on the paddlewheel support arms. Afterwards, vessel representatives posted a small red sign on the port side, but not on the starboard side. And no list could be produced that specifically named authorized personnel.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Photo showing the port paddlewheel support arm. Notice the unprotected sections on the right and left of the photo.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Physical barricades such as warning chains, bars, gates, and railings serve much the same function as safety policies: They provide one more way to keep people from falling prey to their own lapses of memory or judgment. A warning sign, however large and colored, does not provide any physical way to restrict access to a dangerous area. Similarly, barricades such as the chains found hanging on the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST, which are not utilized to protect crew or passengers, are simply useless. Vessel management must place barricades in effective areas of the vessel and then empower supervisors to hold crew accountable for failure to place them in service.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: 3. Rescue effort: After Mr. Staples fell into the water, his subsequent rescue was unsuccessful. Although the efforts of the crew to save him were highly commendable, a number of events transpired to reduce the likelihood that he was rescued in time:

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Lighted deck: An overhead light rests on the port side of the paddlewheel support arms about eight feet up on the accommodation bulkhead. The three witnesses could not agree if it was on at the time of the incident. The light is not part of the rest of the vessel's deck light system, and must be turned on manually from an independent switch inside the garbage room. Some crew members stated that they leave the light in the "off’ position when they go to the stern to smoke, because the added illumination allows personnel supervisors to observe them smoking (in violation of company policy). Others stated that it detracts from the nighttime visibility of passengers sitting in the lounge above the paddlewheel, who complain to management. Investigators determined that, if the light had in fact been left in the off position, Mr. Staples' ability to see the hazards in the immediate environment would have been clearly restricted. Witnesses saw him stumble before going over the side. Had the light been activated, or had the light been part of the rest of the vessel's deck lighting arrangement, Mr. Staples may have avoided tripping in the dark.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: "Free-wheeling" paddlewheel: The river currents around Rainier, OR at the time of the casualty were estimated to be around four knots. The swift-moving waters of the Columbia River were strong enough to permit the cosmetic paddlewheel to begin turning slowly in a "forward" direction. When Mr. Staples slipped, witnesses observed him trying to grasp at the wheel for balance. But instead of finding purchase, the wheel unbalanced him further until he fell into the water. Furthermore, he was observed traveling under the paddlewheel immediately after entering the river, and he may have become injured. A simple safety mechanism preventing the wheel from "free-wheeling" in the current may have permitted him to firmly grasp the unmoving wheel and regain his balance.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Drills and training: According to vessel records, the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST conducted thorough and timely drills, including "Man Overboard" drills. Two of the three crewmen in Mr. Staples' presence at the time of his fall overboard knew exactly what steps to take to ensure the rest of the vessel was alerted to a person in the water. Galley staff member, Mr. however, had never been trained to work with the deckhands to recover a man overboard. Investigators discovered that 40% of crewmembers (mostly stewards and galley staff) do not actively participate in Man Overboard drills or training: Twelve of thity crewmembers did nothing more than simply muster for the drills. The Code of Federal Regulations Subchapter K (46 CFR 122.520) requires that "the master shall conduct drills and instruction to make sure that all crew members are familiar with their duties during the recovery of persons who have fallen overboard." At the time of the fall overboard, Mr. (a member of the galley staff without a Man Overboard Watch Station Bill position) was physically standing closest to Mr. Staples, and he stated that he did not know what actions to take. Mr. and Mr. had to direct him to stay and monitor Mr. Staples' position from the stern.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Additionally, none of the crew could recall any training on procedures to take if they are the individual to fall in the water. Witnesses stated that Mr. Staples appeared to be aware and active, but made no attempt to call out for help, make a flotation device using his clothing, or to attempt a swim to shore. Brief discussions with experienced vessel crew during scheduled training sessions about what to do if a crewmember found him or herself in the water could have been life-saving information for Mr. Staples.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Life rings: The absence of a critical life ring on the port side of the vessel meant that Mr. was unable to find something to throw to Mr. Staples immediately. An empty life ring bracket only forty feet from the stern had once housed a life ring as early as April, 2011. The vessel's crew removed the life ring from service after Coast Guard inspectors noted that it was no longer serviceable. Because the vessel's Certificate of Inspection required only three life rings, Captain stated that replacing the life ring was unnecessary. Despite the fact that regulations required the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST to carry only three life rings, and three were found onboard, investigators noted that Mr. Staples' chances for rescue would have been greater if the empty bracket had contained a life ring. Mr. a trained deckhand, could likely have heaved a life ring to Mr. Staples as he drifted away from the vessel, if one had been available in the bracket for him to use. Instead, the closest life ring was found four decks above at the operating station. By that time, Mr. Staples had drifted too far to reach with a thrown ring.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Photo detailing missing life ring, lowered barrier, and red warning sign.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Neglecting to use the vessel's other life rings may have also contributed to the failure of the rescue effort. Investigators determined that the "Man Overboard" life ring (a life ring equipped with a floating, waterproof light) was not thrown into the water until almost an hour later when the Coast Guard helicopter directed Captain to put it overboard for purposes of datum collection. In a man overboard situation at night, the "Man Overboard" life ring is a critical piece of lifesaving equipment as it serves not only as a point of reference for the alert person in the water to hold for buoyancy, but also as a reference point for rescuers to commence and hone their searching. Without a light in the water in the approximate position of Mr. Staples, rescuers were not afforded an accurate starting reference point.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Investigators noted that the Watch Station Bill did not assign anybody onboard the responsibility of throwing the "Man Overboard" life ring. As a consequence, no one took responsibility for making sure that it had been done so the buoy remained onboard. With proper assignment of duties and follow-on training, this critical piece of life saving gear may have been employed to save a life.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Call for assistance: Captain was awakened at 0108 hrs by Mr. After giving orders for launching the rescue boat and mustering the crew, she immediately contacted the Coast Guard via VHF Channel 16 and local EMS units via cell phone. Shore side assistance arrived at the scene just five minutes after initial notification, and heightened the overall numbers of professional rescuers present.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Analysis
units.content: Rescue boat: Captain and her crew's effort to recover Mr. Staples was further evidenced by the fact that the rescue boat was in the water within five minutes of Mr. Staples' fall overboard. However, the launch of the rescue boat could certainly have been even faster if it had been equipped with a charged searchlight. Instead, Mr. ran up four flights of stairs to reach the navigation bridge in order to obtain suitable lights for the rescue boat crew to use. Although the regulations do not require the rescue boat on the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST to have a searchlight, it remains a critical piece of gear the presence of which may have provided the rescue boat crew the additional time they needed to have saved Mr. Staples.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 1. In accordance with reference (b) the Initiating Event (or first unwanted outcome) for this casualty was Mr. Staples' fall overboard from the port paddlewheel support arm in the area between the aftermost vessel bulkhead and the paddlewheel.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 2. The causal factors that led to the fall overboard are as follows:

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: a) Environment: Although the weather at the time of the incident was relatively benign, the river current speed at the vessel's position in the Columbia River was around 4 knots. Not only did the strong river current cause the paddlewheel to turn in a slow, forward-moving direction, unbalancing Mr. Staples, but it carried him swiftly away from the vessel once he had entered the water. Every minute that Mr. Staples was in the river, he drifted an additional 125 yards from the vessel. Witnesses indicated that they lost sight of him within just a couple of minutes, and by the time the rescue boat was in the water, he was likely half-a-mile downstream.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: b) Organizational Factors: There are three organizational factors that involve American Cruise Lines, Inc. policies and procedures.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 1) Life Jacket Policy: American Cruise Lines, Inc. does not have a policy with respect to life jacket use for personnel working in dangerous areas of the main deck. The majority of the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST's main deck was surrounded by 39 ½ inch high railings with three additional courses to protect passengers and crew. The most dangerous, and least protected, area of the vessel's main deck is the stern. Captain stated that the life jacket policy was only for engineers working on the machinery or the paddlewheel on the stern. Crewmembers handling lines, or anyone else, in the vicinity are not required by policy to wear them. An effective life jacket policy, enforced by the ship's management, would stress the importance of wearing life jackets any time that crewmembers are working in dangerous areas of the vessel, and may have given Mr. Staples good cause for putting on a life jacket prior to approaching the stern.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 2) Station Bill: The P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST's Station Bill does not identify a person to throw the "Man Overboard" life ring. As a consequence, a lighted life ring was not thrown until the vessel was directed by the Coast Guard helicopter around an hour later. Had the Station Bill indicated that a certain crewmember throw the life ring, it would have been done much sooner (probably within a minute or two), and may have given Mr. Staples something to hold for buoyancy while the rescue boat was launched to recover him.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 3) Authorized Personnel: Neither the American Cruise Lines Operations Manual nor the shipboard policies identified which “Authorized Personnel" were permitted access to the stern. As a result, there was confusion onboard with regard to rightful access. When the vessel underwent its cosmetic paddlewheel installation, the Coast Guard and vessel representatives agreed that only engineers would have access to the stern in order to service the hydraulic equipment. The only physical evidence attesting to this agreement was the small red sign placed on the bulkhead leading back to the stern (albeit on the port side only). No formal, written policy or list of designated personnel was ever created to ensure that the policy was followed. And there was no evidence that the rule had ever been formally enforced. Since no document existed to support the captain's claims that personnel should not be loitering on the stern, enforcement of the policy could not easily be made. Furthermore, the ineffective signage and nonexistent physical barriers complicated the captain's ability to enforce the policy. As a result, some of the crewmembers knew they shouldn't be on the stern, some knew the policy wouldn't be enforced if they were, and some didn't even know the policy existed. No crewmembers interviewed could definitively tell investigators if they were “authorized" persons.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: c) Workplace Factors: There are four workplace factors that involve P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST's policies and procedures.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 1) Drills and Training: American Cruise Lines, Inc. provided inadequate training for crewmembers. Though the deckhands were well-trained in the ability to recover a man overboard and launch the rescue boat in a timely fashion, the galley staff and stewards (40% of the crew) had never participated in a man overboard drill beyond simply mustering at the alarm. Furthermore, scheduled man overboard training was provided only for deckhands – galley staff and stewards were not required to attend. As a consequence, Mr. Staples (a member of the galley staff) had never been involved in a man overboard drill, as was true for Mr. Both gentlemen did not know the procedures to take, or how to respond, following a fall overboard. Critical knowledge is passed during training and drill evolutions: This knowledge is vital for all personnel working full-time on a vessel, regardless of their position onboard. All crew should be trained to throw life buoys, alert other crew by shouting, and point/spot for rescuers to find the person in the water.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: Man overboard training should also include information for how to survive a fall into cold water. When Mr. Staples fell overboard, a large pool of crewmembers was not available to assist with the rescue efforts because they had never been trained. Mr. and Mr. provided Mr. verbal directions on the stern immediately after Mr. Staples fell overboard, which resulted in critical seconds lost during the rescue effort.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: On 10 May 2011, during the vessel's last annual inspection, Coast Guard Marine Inspectors drilled the crew on Man Overboard procedures. But according to inspection records, Coast Guard Marine Inspectors did not exercise the vessel's crew in drills during its Certificate of Inspection examination on 13 April 2012. It is unclear whether the deckhands who were onboard when Mr. Staples fell overboard were part of the drill conducted in 2011, but it is not likely. Captain stated that many of the crew are temporary hires, and that they often sign on just prior to the peak summer season. Mr. Staples signed on to the vessel on 28 June 2012, so he had never been observed in a drill by the Coast Guard. Coast Guard Marine Inspectors provide vital experience and training to inspected passenger vessel crewmen. Inspectors should make every effort to visit the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST after the temporary crew has been hired and trained, so that accurate drills can be observed.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 2) Enforcement of Policies. Existing American Cruise Lines, Inc. policies are insufficiently enforced on board P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST. Captain stated that she and the Hotel Manager constantly remind crewmembers to keep clear of the stern, and constantly reinforce that the stern is not a safe place to congregate or loiter. She expressed difficulty enforcing the rule and often had to turn a blind eye to the policy because the crew needed someplace on the vessel to smoke. During the initial Coast Guard visit immediately following the incident, investigators encountered three members of the crew smoking and loitering on the stern when they arrived onboard the vessel. Captain seemed embarrassed by this discovery, but made no action to punish or reprimand the transgressors. She noted that crew members frequently broke another company policy by staying up after midnight. Finally, Captain openly permitted crewmembers to utilize the dining room to play video games despite the "Crew in Quarters after Midnight" policy. She cited that the crew appreciated having the space to congregate together and that it was good for overall morale. Strict enforcement of policy by vessel managers sends a message to employees that breaking the rules is not tolerated. Company rules and policies exist to keep people safe, but without effective enforcement, the rules will be broken, as evidenced in this investigation. Captain and other management staff onboard P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST must take enforcement action against persons who violate safety policies to prevent future incidents.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 3) Barriers: An insufficiency of barriers permitted easy access to the stern by passengers and crew alike. The only physical barriers were "Employees Only" safety chains placed on the main deck walkways to prevent passengers from approaching the stern. But on both Coast Guard visits, investigators found these chains hanging from the bulkhead instead of stretched across the walkways. Captain stated that crewmembers routinely forgot to put these barriers in place. Again, there was no evidence of any consequences for neglectful crew who didn't replace the chains.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 4) Railings: Two sections on the port side stern near the paddlewheel were missing effective railings to prevent a person from falling overboard. Mr. Staples fell through the smaller of the two sections (a 54 inch section). During the cosmetic paddlewheel installation project, Coast Guard and vessel representatives determined that railings in these sections were inappropriate due to the heightened chance of river debris becoming lodged in the railing and damaging vital ship's equipment. The smaller section was left completely exposed, but the larger of the two sections (the ten-foot section) was supposed to be equipped with a chain to warn and prevent personnel from approaching the stern. However, the chain was never fabricated or put in place following the project. The missing smaller railing must be considered to be a causal factor in this case, but the installation of a new railing was not advised due to the increased risk of damage to propulsion equipment.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: d) Personnel: There are three personnel factors related to Mr. Andres Staples.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 1) Alcohol Consumption: According to gathered evidence and witness statements Mr. Staples consumed two mixed drinks (Jack and Coke) and one standard bottle of beer (12 oz.) in a one-hour period. A total of three hours and twenty-five minutes passed from when he signed off the vessel until when he entered the water. Mr. Staples weighed approximately 200 pounds, according to his driver's license. According to most Blood Alcohol Content (BAC) charts and calculators, a 200 pound man who consumed the same amount of alcohol over the same period of time would have a BAC around 0.01%, not enough to legally impair a person. An individual's blood alcohol concentration depends on a variety of additional factors, so it is difficult to accurately assess Mr. Staples' actual levels. Complicating the investigation is the fact that Mr. Staples' whereabouts are unknown for a period of about forty-five minutes between when he signed back on to the vessel and when the first witnesses recount seeing him in the dining room. It is possible that he may have consumed more alcohol on the vessel, but not likely, as alcohol containers were not found on his person or in his personal effects. Without further evience or witness testimony that Mr. Staples consumed additional alcohol, his blood alcohol content cannot be assumed to be at a level to impair him.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 2) Violation of Safety Policies: American Cruise Lines, Inc. had several safety policies in place that could have effectively prevented this incident if Mr. Staples had been following them. Mr. Staples was made aware of the policies when he signed on to work as a galley steward. Had Mr. Staples abided by the "Crew in Quarters after Midnight" policy, he would have been in his berth instead of on the stern. Furthermore, had he been following the "No Smoking" policy, he would have gone to shore to smoke instead of placing himself in a hazardous area of the vessel. Finally, Mr. Staples violated the "No Alcohol"policy by consuming alcohol earlier that night.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 3) Fatigue: Historically, marine casualty investigations have shown that fatigue often contributes to errors in judgment and attention failures. In this case, it cannot be conclusively determined if fatigue was a factor in Mr. Staples' fall overboard, but the likelihood that Mr. Staples was suffering from fatigue is high. At the end of his shift, he was relieved by Mr. at around 2150 hrs because "he had wanted to go for a drink," according to witnesses. Mr. Staples spent about two hours on shore and returned to the vessel, where he stayed up playing video games with other off-duty crew. He fell overboard shortly after 0100 hrs. "Al three witnesses saw him slip on the step when he approached the paddlewheel, one witness saw him slip twice. He was also observed to fumble with clutching at the paddlewheel boards before falling off the vessel. Although witnesses were unable to tell investigators exactly how long Mr. Staples had been awake, it can be safely inferred through witness statements that fatigue played a role in his fall overboard.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: e) Safety Equipment:

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 1) Deck Lighting: Although witnesses conflicted as to whether the flood light was on at the time of the incident, the fact that the light was wired on a separate switch from the rest of the deck lights allowed investigators to reasonably conclude that the light was likely off at the time of the fall. Additionally, by leaving the switch in the "off' position, a certain degree of concealment at night is afforded to unauthorized persons wishing to remain unseen by vessel managers and passengers. Although witnesses were able to see Mr. Staples in the water clearly enough to know that his eyes were open and that he was moving his arms in the water, bright lights flooded the area from the grain facility across the river which may have provided an extra degree of illumination. But had the light definitively been in operation, Mr. Staples may have had enough illumination to see his surroundings, and a fall could have been avoided.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 3. The causal factors that existed during the rescue efforts are as follows:

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: a) Safety Equipment:

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 1) Searchlight: The Code of Federal Regulations does not require "K-Boat" passenger vessels to equip their rescue boats with searchlights. The P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST's rescue boat had onboard a box labeled "Searchlight" though no searchlight was included in the rescue boat's outfit. Nobody onboard could clarify if a searchlight had ever been part of the rescue boat's equipment. Because Mr. Staples fell overboard in the middle of the night, the launch of the rescue boat was delayed as Mr. ran to the 4thDeck Operating Station in order to find two suitable flashlights for boat crew rescuers to utilize for searching.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 2) Life Ring: Mr. also ran past an empty life ring bracket on his way to find something to throw to Mr. Staples. He was not aware of an empty life ring bracket on the main deck becaușe he signed on to the vessel after the life ring had already been removed due to deterioration. The missing life ring had been condemned for multiple cracks by Mr. during an inspection which occurred in the same timeframe as the cosmetic paddlewheel installation. The inspector noted the deficiency with the life ring (as well as several other lesser deficiencies on the other life rings) to the vessel's representative, Mr. and advised him to repair the life rings. Despite the missing life ring, the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST was still well-within the operating limitations of its Certificate of Inspection, which only required three life rings. Since the vessel had a total of four other functional life rings onboard, and was already repairing the other life rings, a requirement for a new life ring was not issued to the vessel. Mr. disposed of the condemned life ring, as it was no longer serviceable.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 3) Life Jacket: Mr. Staples was not wearing a life jacket at the time of his fall overboard. Had he been wearing a Coast Guard approved life jacket, he may have remained afloat to be safely rescued.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 4. There is no evidence of misconduct, inattention to duty, or negligent or willful violation of law or regulation on the part of American Cruise Lines, Inc., licensed or certificated personnel, or Coast Guard personnel.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 5. There is no evidence of failure to properly respond to this situation by American Cruise Lines, Inc., the crew of the Passenger Vessel QUEEN OF THE WEST, the U. S. Coast Guard or any other responsible agency.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Conclusions
units.content: 6. There is no evidence that any personnel of the Coast Guard or of any other agency or any other person contributed to this casualty.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content:
Safety
1. Recommend that the Commandant of the Coast Guard consider requiring life rings with lights on both sides of the main deck and searchlights in rescue boats as part of Subchapter K Regulations.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 2. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. test random crew members in Man Overboard drills annually. Coast Guard Marine Inspectors should plan to conduct a scheduled drill with the crew at the earliest convenience to the vessel after all temporary summer employees and deckhands have been hired and have had a chance to become familiar with the vessel.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 3. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. develop an inclusive safety policy with regard to all crew wearing life jackets while working in the vicinity of the stern. American Cruise Lines, Inc. should consider required personal protective equipment, safety practices, buddy system, and/or tie-off system in developing their policy.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 4. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. assign all crew members a duty during a man overboard event and document these duties on the Station Bill.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 5. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. update the Station Bill to assign one crew member the responsibility of throwing the “Man Overboard" life buoy in event of a fall overboard. This person should have other duties on or near the bridge. All crew should be trained to throw anything buoyant immediately available to assist a person in the water.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 6. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. place a serviceable searchlight in the rescue boat.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 7. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. place a serviceable life ring in the port side main deck life ring bracket.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 8. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. provide floating lights for all main deck life rings.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 9. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. develop an inclusive safety policy with regard to authorized crew permitted to work on the stern in the vicinity of the paddlewheel. The policy should designate in writing the “authorized persons" permitted in the area and detail specific evolutions requiring access (ie. trash detail, mooring/sea detail, maintenance, etc.). A physical list of authorized persons would deter others from accessing this dangerous area of the vessel, and provide an effective tool to enforce the policy.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 10. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc. provide physical barriers such as chains and warning signs on both sides of the vessel as visual deterrents to prevent unauthorized access to the stern.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 11. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc., in consultation with U.S. Coast Guard Marine Safety Unit Portland Inspection Department, install effective deck lights (wired to the main deck lighting controls) on the stern portion of the vessel. In the meaņtime, it is recommended that P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST crew activate existing stern lights from sunset to sunrise every night.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 12. It is recommended that American Cruise Lines, Inc., in consultation with U.S. Coast Guard Marine Safety Unit Portland Inspection Department, consider developing a locking mechanism to prevent the movement of the paddlewheel during swift current conditions. The mechanism should be developed only if the risk of damage to the paddlewheel support arms or associated vessel propulsion machinery is minimized.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 13. It is recommended that the Master of P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST provide survival training and Man Overboard training for all crew following a fall into the water.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 14. It is recommended that the Master of P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST ensure all crew actively participate in drills to ensure knowledge of man overboard recovery procedures.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 15. It is recommended that the Master of P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST actively enforce the “authorized personnel only" policy to prevent others from accessing the stern of the vessel. Enforcement should include the use of effective and appropriate punishment and/or documentation of all personnel who violate the policy.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 16. It is recommended that the Master of P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST actively enforce all American Cruise Lines, Inc. Operations Manual policies onboard P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST, but most notably the following:

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: a. No drinking. Enforcement could include random alcohol tests when crew return from shore.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: b. Crew in quarters after midnight. Enforcement could include watchmen keeping track of who is not in quarters after midnight.

units.parent_chunk: Investigating Officer's Report > Recommendations
units.content: 17. It is recommended that P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST's Engineer design (and put in place) a safety chain protecting authorized personnel on the paddlewheel support arms from falling from the stern in the area of the ten-foot railing gap.

units.content:
Other
